title: Hagar, Seen in the Desert
overview: Hagar, an enslaved Egyptian woman, is used to give Abram an heir, is mistreated and runs away, and is met in the desert by God, who hears her suffering and promises her a son.

parts.label: Sarai's plan (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: After ten childless years in Canaan, Sarai uses a custom known from the ancient Near East: a childless wife could give her slave to her husband and count the child as her own. Hagar becomes a secondary wife while still a slave, and the text never records what she wanted.

parts.label: Contempt, blame and flight (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: Once pregnant, Hagar looks down on Sarai, Sarai blames Abram, and Abram hands Hagar back to Sarai's control. Sarai treats her harshly, with a Hebrew word later used for Egypt oppressing Israel, and Hagar runs.

parts.label: Found at a desert spring (vv. 7-9)
parts.note: On the road toward Egypt, her homeland, the angel of the LORD finds her and is the first to call her by name; in verse 13 she treats him as God himself. His order to go back and submit is hard to read: some see it as saving a pregnant woman from the desert, others as accepting her slavery.

parts.label: A promise and a name (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: The angel promises Hagar countless descendants and names her son Ishmael, meaning 'God hears,' because God has heard her misery. Verse 12 likens him to a wild donkey ('wild ass' in older translations), a picture of untamed desert freedom amid conflict, and its last line is unclear, rendered either as living 'in hostility toward' or 'over against' his brothers.

parts.label: Hagar names God (vv. 13-14)
parts.note: Hagar calls God El Roi, which translations render 'the God who sees me' or 'a God that sees,' and she is often noted as the only person in the Bible to give God a name. The Hebrew of her next words is uncertain, and the well's name, Beer Lahai Roi, roughly means 'well of the Living One who sees me.'

parts.label: Ishmael is born (vv. 15-16)
parts.note: The story implies Hagar went back, and Ishmael is born when Abram is 86; Abram gives him the name the angel chose. Ishmael appears again in chapter 17, and Hagar's story continues in chapter 21.

disagreement: Christians differ on where this chapter's weight falls: many older readers see it mainly as Abram and Sarai failing to wait for God's promise, with Hagar rightly sent back, while many modern readers center Hagar as an abused enslaved woman whom God sees, and they read the command to return as either protective or deeply troubling.
think: Hagar goes back to the same hard household, yet the story treats being seen and heard as something that changes her; what difference, if any, can being truly seen make when circumstances stay the same?
